summary: This bill amends 18 U.S.C. § 242 to explicitly cover the use of force during responses to protests as a deprivation of rights under color of law and removes the death penalty as a possible sentence.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends a criminal statute (18 USC 242) to clarify penalties for deprivation of rights under color of law, specifically including use of force at protests, and removes the death penalty option. It contains no provisions related to federal budgets, appropriations, or expenditures.
The bill makes no changes to tax law, rates, deductions, or enforcement mechanisms.
No provisions address healthcare policy, insurance, providers, or public health programs.
The bill does not regulate firearms, use of force standards for civilians, or gun ownership rights.
No references to immigration, border policy, visas, or enforcement against non-citizens.
The legislation does not address reproductive rights, abortion access, or related regulations.
No provisions affect military funding, defense policy, or armed forces operations.
The bill contains nothing related to environmental regulations, emissions, or conservation.
No changes to welfare programs, food assistance, or entitlement benefits.
No provisions touch on schools, federal education funding, or school choice.
The bill does not address controlled substances, decriminalization, or drug enforcement.

The bill directly amends 18 USC 242 (deprivation of rights under color of law) to explicitly cover use of force during protest responses and eliminates the death penalty option. This strengthens accountability for law enforcement misconduct at protests, aligning with criminal justice reform and rehabilitation rather than tougher sentencing.
No provisions relate to tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
The bill has no fiscal impact or provisions addressing deficits or debt reduction.
No language concerning LGBTQ protections, discrimination, or legal status.
No references to foreign assistance, international aid, or State Department programs.
The bill does not address voting rights, election administration, or voter ID.
No provisions on data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance.
While protests can relate to labor actions, the bill makes no changes to labor law, union rights, or worker protections.
The bill does not address religious exemptions, civil rights enforcement, or anti-discrimination law.
